These elements reflect a sophisticated application of epidemiological modeling and evaluation techniques. The primary focus is not on describing a single outbreak, estimating immunity, or forecasting outcomes in real time, but on developing and applying a structured analytical framework to evaluate how multiple systems (epidemiological, climatic, demographic) interact to shape disease burden. This makes Class 5 the most appropriate, as it best supports multi-step inference questions involving model assumptions, causal inference, bias correction, and the interpretation of complex statistical relationships across domains.

This challenges assumptions about co-evolution and reservoir competence. The passage thus focuses on the mechanistic underpinnings of host susceptibility and immune activation, which are core to Class 4. Multi-step inference questions could explore how evolutionary history shapes immune responses, why certain cell types resist infection despite receptor expression, or how cytokine hubs like CCL5 and IL6 might influence transmission potential—requiring integration of virology, immunology, and evolutionary biology.
